headings.title: Introduction to HIV/AIDS Pathophysiology and Immune Suppression
headings.content: Human Immunodeficiency Virus specifically targets the immune system, entering and destroying **CD4+ T helper cells**. These cells act as the commanders of the body's defense network, signaling other immune cells to fight off invading germs. As the virus replicates inside the CD4+ cells, it gradually reduces their population. When the CD4+ cell count drops below **200 cells per microliter**, or when an individual develops an AIDS-defining condition, the disease progresses to **Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS)**. Without a strong cell-mediated response, the body loses its ability to defend itself against everyday pathogens that a healthy immune system easily clears.

headings.title: Opportunistic Infections Associated with Advanced HIV
headings.content:
When immune surveillance fails, microorganisms that normally cause no harm in healthy people can cause severe, life-threatening illness. These are known as **opportunistic infections**. Nurses must recognize the common presentations of these infections in patients with advanced disease:

- **Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)**: A fungal lung infection causing progressive dry cough, fever, and severe shortness of breath on exertion.
- **Oral Candidiasis (Thrush)**: A fungal overgrowth on the mucous membranes of the mouth and tongue, presenting as creamy white patches that scrape off to reveal bleeding mucosa.
- **Cryptococcal Meningitis**: A fungal infection spreading to the brain coverings, leading to severe headache, fever, and confusion.
- **Toxoplasmosis**: A parasitic infection forming brain lesions that cause focal neurological deficits, headaches, and seizures.
- **Cytomegalovirus (CMV)**: A viral infection that frequently attacks the retina, potentially causing permanent blindness, as well as affecting the gastrointestinal tract.

headings.title: HIV-Associated Malignancies and Cancers
headings.content:
The persistent loss of immune control allows abnormal cells to multiply unchecked, leading to specific malignancies classified as AIDS-defining conditions. 

- **Kaposi Sarcoma**: A vascular tumor caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8). It presents as firm, painless, purplish or brownish skin lesions, and can also spread internally to the lungs and gastrointestinal tract.
- **Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma**: Aggressive lymphomas, often originating in B cells, frequently presenting in extranodal sites like the central nervous system or the gastrointestinal tract.
- **Invasive Cervical Cancer**: Linked to persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, progressing much faster and behaving more aggressively in women living with HIV.

headings.title: Neurological and Cognitive Complications
headings.content: The central nervous system is a frequent target for both the HIV virus itself and secondary infections. **HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND)** encompasses a spectrum of conditions ranging from mild mental slowing and poor concentration to severe, debilitating dementia. Patients may experience memory loss, apathy, and balance difficulties. Direct viral invasion of the brain and chronic neuroinflammation drive these cognitive changes. Additionally, opportunistic infections like toxoplasmosis and cryptococcal meningitis can cause acute neurological emergencies characterized by severe headaches, altered mental status, and focal deficits.

headings.title: Metabolic and Cardiovascular Complications
headings.content: Long-term survival with HIV, combined with the metabolic effects of certain antiretroviral medications, has shifted the clinical picture toward chronic systemic diseases. Patients face an elevated risk of **cardiovascular disease**, including myocardial infarction and stroke, driven by persistent systemic inflammation and dyslipidemia. **Lipodystrophy**—characterized by abnormal fat redistribution, such as fat accumulation around the abdomen and buffalo hump formation alongside wasting in the face and limbs—is a well-known metabolic complication. Insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes are also more prevalent, requiring careful blood glucose monitoring and dietary management.

headings.title: Psychosocial Complications and Mental Health Challenges
headings.content: Living with a chronic, stigmatized condition profoundly impacts psychological well-being. Depression and anxiety are exceptionally common among individuals diagnosed with HIV, often exacerbated by fear of disclosure, societal discrimination, and the daily burden of lifelong medication management. **Stigma** remains a major barrier to care, frequently leading to social isolation and treatment non-adherence. Nurses must screen for mood disorders, assess coping mechanisms, and connect patients with support groups and mental health professionals to ensure holistic recovery.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Monitoring for HIV Complications
headings.content: Rigorous, systematic assessment is vital to catch secondary complications before they become life-threatening. Nurses monitor two primary laboratory values: **CD4+ cell count**, which indicates the health and strength of the immune system, and **viral load**, which measures the amount of active virus circulating in the blood. A successful treatment goal is an **undetectable viral load**, which protects health and prevents sexual transmission. Clinical assessments must also include routine screening for opportunistic infections through weight tracking, respiratory evaluation, neurological checks, and skin inspections.

headings.title: Comprehensive Nursing Management and Patient Education
headings.content: Holistic nursing care focuses on promoting lifelong adherence to **antiretroviral therapy (ART)**, managing drug side effects, and preventing new infections. Because missing doses allows the virus to mutate and develop drug resistance, education must emphasize strict medication compliance. Nurses teach patients about safe food and water practices to avoid foodborne opportunistic infections, encourage up-to-date vaccinations against pneumococcus and influenza, and provide counseling on safer sex practices. Empowering the patient with practical self-management tools transforms chronic disease management into a collaborative partnership.
